title: Plugin types: ESM, ESP and ESL (light plugins)
content:
Plugin types: ESM, ESP and ESL (light plugins)
Fallout 4 loads three kinds of plugin file. All three use the same record format; what differs is two flags in the file header (the TES4 record) and how the game numbers their records.
- ESM (master): header flag 0x1 set. Fallout4.esm and the DLC .esm files are masters. Masters load before regular plugins.
- ESP (regular plugin): no master flag. Most mods are ESPs.
- ESL (light plugin): header flag 0x200 set. A light plugin can be a file with the .esl extension or a normal .esp/.esm with the light (ESL) flag set. Light plugins do NOT take one of the full load-order slots.
Load-order limit: full plugins (ESM/ESP) use load-order indexes 0x00-0xFD, so at most 254 full plugins can be active. Index 0xFE is reserved for light plugins, which all load under that one index, so ESL-flagging small mods is how players get past the 254 limit.
Rule of thumb for a beginner: make your mod an ESL (or an ESL-flagged ESP) when it adds few enough new records (see "ESL record limits"); keep it a full ESP/ESM when it adds more.
tags: plugins esl esp esm light-plugin load-order limits header-flags
verified_by: Header flags read from the real plugins in Fallout 4\Data (Fallout4.esm and DLC .esm have 0x1; Bethesda Creation Club vchgs002fo4_bountyhunter.esl has 0x200). 254-slot rule matches FactGuard.ts.

title: ESL (light plugin) record limits: 2,048 or 4,095 new records, depending on the header version
content:
ESL (light plugin) record limits: 2,048 or 4,095 new records, depending on the header version
A light plugin's own new records must use object IDs no higher than 0xFFF. How low they may start depends on the plugin's header version (HEDR):
- Header version 1.0 (what current Creation Kit builds save): new records may use object IDs 0x001-0xFFF, so a light plugin can add up to 4,095 new records.
- Header version 0.95 (older plugins): new records start at 0x800, so the range is 0x800-0xFFF: up to 2,048 new records.
Records that only override other plugins' records (edits of vanilla or DLC records) do not count toward this limit; only records the plugin itself adds do.
If a plugin's new records use IDs above 0xFFF, it cannot be ESL-flagged until they are renumbered: in xEdit, right-click the plugin and use "Compact FormIDs for ESL", then set the ESL flag in the file header. Only compact BEFORE you release the mod: renumbering changes the FormIDs that existing saves refer to, so compacting an already-released plugin breaks players' saves.
Common mistake: the often-quoted rule "ESL FormIDs must be 0x800-0xFFF" is only true for the old 0.95 header.
tags: esl light-plugin formid limits compact xedit header-version 4095 2048
verified_by: Measured from real plugins in Fallout 4\Data: Bethesda's light plugin vchgs002fo4_bountyhunter.esl (header 1.0) has 3,883 new records with object IDs 0x001-0xF3D; every header-0.95 plugin's new records start at 0x800; Fallout4.esm (header 1.0) starts at 0x001. The xEdit compaction command and the save-breaking warning come from Mossy's guides.

title: SEQ files: why a Start Game Enabled quest doesn't start on an existing save
content:
SEQ files: why a Start Game Enabled quest doesn't start on an existing save
A SEQ file is a small binary file that lists the quests a plugin adds that have "Start Game Enabled" ticked. The game uses it to start those quests in a save that already exists. If your plugin adds Start Game Enabled quests and has no SEQ file, those quests may never start for anyone who loads an existing save (the classic "my quest doesn't start" bug).
What is inside: only the FormIDs of the plugin's OWN new Start Game Enabled quests, 4 bytes each. Vanilla quests your plugin only edits are not in it.
Where it goes: a folder named SEQ next to the plugin, with the plugin's name: Data\SEQ\MyMod.seq for MyMod.esp. In Mod Organizer 2 that is <your mod folder>\seq\MyMod.seq.
How to make it:
1. xEdit (FO4Edit): load your plugin, right-click it and choose "Create SEQ File".
2. Creation Kit: the CK has a SEQ exporter that writes SEQ\<plugin>.SEQ; it is run with the -GenerateSEQ command-line switch.
Regenerate the SEQ file whenever you add or remove Start Game Enabled quests.
To test a quest right now in your own game without a SEQ file, use the console: StartQuest <QuestEditorID> (see "Quest console commands").
tags: seq quest start-game-enabled existing-save xedit creation-kit
verified_by: Two real mods from the MO2 mods folder (We People Can Live In, Necessity) checked byte by byte: each SEQ file is exactly the FormIDs of that plugin's own new Start Game Enabled quests (QUST DNAM flag 0x0001); Necessity's 8 overridden vanilla Start Game Enabled quests are absent. The seq\<plugin>.seq layout is used by both. FO4xEdit64.exe contains the "Create SEQ File" command; CreationKit.exe contains -GenerateSEQ, a SEQExporter and the output path SEQ\%s.SEQ.

title: Quest console commands for testing (StartQuest, SetStage and others)
content:
Quest console commands for testing (StartQuest, SetStage and others)
Open the console in game with the ~ key. Quest commands take the quest's Editor ID (or FormID):
- StartQuest <quest>: start a quest that is not running.
- StopQuest <quest>: stop it.
- ResetQuest <quest>: reset it to its starting state.
- CompleteQuest <quest>: mark it complete.
- SetStage <quest> <stage>: jump to a stage, for example SetStage MyQuest 10.
- GetStage <quest>: show the current stage.
- ShowQuestStages <quest>: list the quest's stages and which are done.
- SetObjectiveDisplayed <quest> <objective> 1 and CompleteAllObjectives <quest>: objective control.
There is no "SetQuest" command.
These are for testing. Players should not need the console: if a Start Game Enabled quest does not start on existing saves, ship a SEQ file (see "SEQ files").
tags: console quest startquest setstage testing debugging
verified_by: Each command name checked as a string in the real Fallout4.exe: StartQuest, SetStage, StopQuest, CompleteQuest, ResetQuest, GetStage, ShowQuestStages, SetObjectiveDisplayed and CompleteAllObjectives are present; SetQuest is absent.

title: Precombines and previs: what they are and why mods "break" them
content:
Precombines and previs: what they are and why mods "break" them
Precombined meshes (precombines): to save draw calls, the game merges many static objects in a cell (walls, rubble, rocks) into a few combined meshes. Vanilla ships them in Meshes\PreCombined\ (181,611 .nif files in the base game). Instead of drawing hundreds of separate objects, the game draws a few combined ones.
Previs (precomputed visibility): data that tells the game which parts of a cell can be seen from where, so it can skip drawing what is hidden. Vanilla stores it as .uvd files in the Vis\ folder (1,360 in the base game).
Why mods "break previs": if your plugin moves, deletes, adds or edits a static object inside a precombined cell, the game can no longer use that cell's combined meshes and visibility data. It falls back to drawing every object separately, which costs a lot of FPS and can cause flickering or objects popping in and out. Players call this "broken precombines" or "broken previs".
How to avoid or fix it:
- Avoid editing static objects in precombined exterior cells when you can.
- If you must, regenerate precombines and previs for the cells you changed and ship them with your mod. The Creation Kit does this with its "PreCombine Geometry For World" and previs generation options (on the command line: -GeneratePreCombined and -GeneratePreVisData). It writes the new meshes to Data\Meshes\PreCombined\. Pack the generated files into your mod's archive.
- When several mods in a load order break precombines, players use a patch such as PRP (Previsibines Repair Pack), or Mossy's previs workflow in the Plugin & Load Order Hub.
tags: precombine previs uvd vis fps performance creation-kit prp
verified_by: Counted in the extracted vanilla game data: Meshes\PreCombined has 181,611 .nif files; Vis has 1,360 .uvd files. CreationKit.exe contains -GeneratePreCombined, -GeneratePreVisData, "PreCombine Geometry For World", "Update PreCombine/PreVis Timestamp" and the output path Data\Meshes\PreCombined\%s.NIF.

title: BA2 archives: General vs Textures, what goes inside, and naming
content:
BA2 archives: General vs Textures, what goes inside, and naming
A .ba2 file is Fallout 4's archive format: many game files packed into one, which loads faster than thousands of loose files.
Two kinds:
- General (GNRL): meshes (.nif), scripts (.pex), sounds and music, voice files (.fuz), animations (.hkx), materials, interface files, SEQ files and anything else that is not a texture.
- Textures (DX10): only .dds textures, stored in a texture-specific layout. Textures must go in a Textures archive, not a General one.
Naming: an archive loads with the plugin of the same name: MyMod.esp loads "MyMod - Main.ba2" (General) and "MyMod - Textures.ba2" (Textures). Bethesda's own files follow the same pattern (DLCCoast - Main.ba2, DLCCoast - Textures.ba2, DLCCoast - Voices_en.ba2).
Make them with Archive2.exe (in Fallout 4\Tools\Archive2) or Mossy's packaging tools: choose the General format for non-texture files and DX10 for textures.
tags: ba2 archive archive2 general dx10 textures packaging naming
verified_by: All 38 BA2 headers in Fallout 4\Data read: 21 GNRL and 17 DX10; every DX10 archive holds only .dds; GNRL archives hold .nif, .pex, .hkx, .fuz, .btr and more. In the MO2 mods folder 468 of 469 "<name> - Main/Textures.ba2" archives sit next to a plugin of exactly that name.

title: Papyrus script files: where .psc sources and compiled .pex files go
content:
Papyrus script files: where .psc sources and compiled .pex files go
Papyrus scripts exist in two forms:
- Source (.psc): the text you write. Your own sources go in Data\Scripts\Source\User\. Bethesda's vanilla sources are in Data\Scripts\Source\Base\ (installed with the Creation Kit), with DLC sources in Source\DLC01 to DLC06.
- Compiled (.pex): what the game actually runs. Compiled scripts go in Data\Scripts\ (subfolders follow the script's namespace). The base game ships 2,422 of them.
The Creation Kit's compiler (PapyrusCompiler.exe) turns .psc into .pex. A script attached to a record in your plugin does nothing in game unless its .pex file ships with the mod (loose in Scripts\ or inside your General BA2). Source files are optional for players but helpful to other modders.
tags: papyrus psc pex compile scripts source user base
verified_by: Folders read in the real install: Fallout 4\Data\Scripts\Source has Base (2,424 .psc), CreationClub, DLC01-DLC06 and User; the extracted vanilla Scripts folder holds 2,422 .pex.

title: Load order rules: masters, patches and the Bashed Patch
content:
Load order rules: masters, patches and the Bashed Patch
- A plugin must load after every master it depends on (its masters are listed in its file header). Missing or out-of-order masters crash the game at startup.
- When two plugins edit the same record, the one loaded LAST wins for that whole record.
- A compatibility patch for mods A and B must load after both; loaded earlier, its changes are immediately overridden and it does nothing.
- Leveled lists (LVLI, LVLN, LVSP) from several mods only combine if you build a merged patch, for example Wrye Bash's Bashed Patch. The Bashed Patch goes last and must be rebuilt whenever you add, remove, update or reorder mods; an outdated one can merge removed or old records.
- Navmesh edits cannot be merged: when two mods edit the same navmesh, only one version can win, and conflicts can crash the game. Use a compatibility patch that carries the winning navmesh.
- LOOT can sort most load orders automatically; read its warnings.
tags: load-order masters patches bashed-patch wrye-bash loot leveled-lists navmesh
verified_by: Rules from Mossy's Plugin & Load Order Hub; these are behaviour rules, not checkable against files. Master dependency follows the record format read from real plugins (MAST entries in the TES4 header).

title: NPC voice files: .fuz, .lip and how they are named
content:
NPC voice files: .fuz, .lip and how they are named
Each spoken dialogue line needs a voice file named after the dialogue response it belongs to: 00 + the INFO record's object ID + _ + the response number, for example 0001A6A0_1.fuz. The response number is the one stored in the INFO record's response data (TRDA). Dialogue (DIAL) and response (INFO) records sit inside the quest's record groups, so the quest and dialogue records must exist before voice files can be named.
- .fuz: the game's voice format, audio with lip-sync data packed in. Some vanilla .fuz files contain no lip data.
- .lip: the lip-sync data on its own (made by the Creation Kit's LipGen, or tools such as Runalip).
Voice files go in Sound\Voice\<PluginName>\<VoiceType>\, usually inside a General BA2 (Bethesda ships them in "<plugin> - Voices_en.ba2").
